title: Bearings & Shafts
summary: Bearing types, L10 fatigue life and equivalent load rating, plus combined bending-torsion shaft design for rotating assemblies.

sections.heading: The Rotating Joint
sections.content:
A bearing is the machine element that permits **relative rotation with low, predictable friction** while carrying load. Its selection is one of the most consequential decisions in machine design: it sets the shaft size, housing geometry, lubrication, and the machine's service life. Bearings fail by **fatigue spalling** (material flaking off raceways), by contamination wear, and by misinstallation — in that rough order of frequency.

The design loop couples bearing and shaft: the shaft needs a diameter the bearing can mount on (see [[iso-fits-and-surface-finish|ISO fits]]), and the bearing load determines the reactions the shaft must survive.

sections.heading: Choosing the Bearing Type
sections.content:
Match the bearing to the dominant load direction and misalignment:

| Type | Carries | Typical use |
|---|---|---|
| Deep-groove ball | Radial + moderate axial | General purpose, high speed |
| Angular-contact ball | Combined radial + axial | Gear shafts, preloaded pairs |
| Cylindrical roller | High radial | Medium-heavy shafts |
| Spherical roller | Heavy radial + misalignment | Mills, crushers, fans |
| Tapered roller | High combined radial + axial | Automotive hubs, gearboxes |
| Thrust ball/roller | Primarily axial | Screw drives, vertical shafts |

Selection order: decide the **axial capacity** needed (does the shaft push against something?), the radial load magnitude, speed (rolling-element bearings have speed limits per the manufacturer's n·dM reference), and misalignment tolerance. A spherical or self-aligning bearing forgives housing bore alignment errors; a rigid deep-groove does not.

sections.heading: L10 Fatigue Life
sections.content:
Rolling-element bearings are rated by the **basic dynamic load rating C** — the constant radial load under which 90% of an apparently identical bearing population survives 1 million revolutions. The **basic rating life** is:

$$L_{10} = \left( \frac{C}{P} \right)^p \times 10^6 \text{ revolutions}$$

with $p = 3$ for ball bearings and $p = 10/3$ for roller bearings. In hours:

$$L_{10h} = \frac{10^6}{60 \, n} \left( \frac{C}{P} \right)^p$$

Example: a bearing with $C = 29.5$ kN carrying $P = 8$ kN at 1500 rpm:

$$L_{10} = \left( \frac{29.5}{8} \right)^3 \times 10^6 = 50.2 \times 10^6 \text{ rev} \quad \rightarrow \quad L_{10h} = \frac{50.2 \times 10^6}{60 \times 1500} = 558 \, \text{hours}$$

Double the load and life drops to 1/8 — bearing life is brutally load-sensitive, which is why preload and alignment (see fatigue basics in [[fatigue-and-failure-analysis|fatigue & failure]]) matter so much.

sections.heading: Equivalent Dynamic Load
sections.content:
Real bearings carry **combined radial and axial loads**. The rating equation uses an equivalent load:

$$P = XF_r + YF_a$$

where $F_r$ is radial and $F_a$ axial force, and $X$, $Y$ are factors from the bearing table determined by the ratio $F_a/F_r$ versus a threshold $e$. Rules of thumb:

- If $F_a / F_r \leq e$: pure radial treatment, $X = 1$, $Y = 0$ (axial load negligible).
- Beyond the threshold, $X$, $Y$ come from the manufacturer's table per bearing series.
- Never forget **dynamic effects**: transmitted gear forces change direction as the gear rotates, so use the maximum resultant, and include rotor unbalance and gyroscopic moments on high-speed shafts.

Preloaded bearing pairs (DB/DF mounting) change the effective $P$; follow the application engineering guidance for the specific pair configuration.

sections.heading: Shaft Design: Bending + Torsion
sections.content:
A shaft carries bending moment $M$ (from transverse loads — gears, belt pull) and torque $T$ (from power transmission). Combined stress is handled by **von Mises**:

$$\sigma_v = \sqrt{\sigma_b^2 + 3\tau_t^2} \leq \frac{S_y}{n}$$

with $\sigma_b = 32M/(\pi d^3)$ and $\tau_t = 16T/(\pi d^3)$ for a solid circular shaft.

Example: shaft Ø30 mm with $M = 120$ N·m, $T = 200$ N·m:

$$\sigma_b = \frac{32 \times 120\,000}{\pi \times 30^3} = 45.3 \text{ MPa}, \qquad \tau_t = \frac{16 \times 200\,000}{\pi \times 30^3} = 37.7 \text{ MPa}$$
$$\sigma_v = \sqrt{45.3^2 + 3 \times 37.7^2} = 79.5 \text{ MPa}$$

Design practice: size the shaft for **fatigue** (stress concentrations at shoulders, keyways, and fillets dominate — see [[fatigue-and-failure-analysis|fatigue]]), pick the bearing bore to match, then re-check the shaft deflection at bearings (angular misalignment limit ≈ 0.04° for ball bearings) and the critical speed.

sections.heading: Fits, Locking & Mounting
sections.content:
Rotation and forces transfer through the **interference fit** between bearing inner ring and shaft, and outer ring and housing:

- Inner ring on shaft: rotating load → **k6, m6** (light interference); shaft stationary and load rotating → j6, h6.
- Outer ring in housing: rotating outer ring → **M7, N7**; stationary outer ring with local loading → H7.
- **H7/k6** is the everyday default for ball bearings in general machinery; deviate only with a documented reason (see [[iso-fits-and-surface-finish|ISO fits]]).

Mounting rules: press on the **ring that turns** (never transmit force through the balls), support the inner ring when pressing onto a shaft, use an oil bath or induction heater for larger bearings (max ~110 °C), and fit seals properly — see [[springs-seals-and-keys|springs, seals & keys]] for keyway load transfer and seal selection that completes the assembly.

keyTakeaways: L10 life is load to the 3rd power (balls) or 10/3 (rollers): L10 = (C/P)^p × 10^6 rev.
Select bearing type by axial capacity, load magnitude, speed, and misalignment tolerance.
Size shafts with von Mises combined bending-torsion, then check deflection and critical speed.
Mount by pressing the rotating ring; use k6/m6 shaft fits and H7 housing fits as the default.
